blocks.text: Finding the right icon required knowing the right word

Designers used approved icons every day, but the repository they depended on had been created in 2001. It loaded slowly, lacked useful version information and returned poor search results unless someone already knew the system's terminology.

That friction affected more than speed. When people could not find or verify the approved asset, they reused an old file, created a replacement or searched elsewhere. The repository was meant to protect consistency, yet its own experience encouraged design debt.
Sometimes I do not know what words to use for searching. The most obvious ones do not work.

blocks.text: Search was only one part of the service

I conducted five interviews and surveyed the wider design and development community. The research covered how people searched, what information they needed after downloading an asset and what happened when the asset did not exist.

The missing request path proved as important as search. People did not know who owned a new icon, how long creation would take or how to flag a problem with an existing asset. Improving the search box without addressing that lifecycle would only solve the easiest part of the experience.

items: Can I find the approved asset using language that makes sense to me?
Can I see its status, version and intended use?
Can I report a problem or request something new?
Can the people maintaining the library review and publish changes safely?

blocks.text: I mapped the service from discovery and download through requests, review and publication. The blueprint helped designers, asset owners and technical stakeholders agree on responsibilities that the old interface had left invisible.

blocks.alt: Service blueprint for the proposed asset repository
blocks.caption: The service blueprint connected the visible repository to the review and maintenance work behind it.

blocks.text: The interface needed structured information for tags, search terms, version history, usage guidance and approval status. A conventional content-management build would have added time and dependencies before we knew whether the experience worked.

I proposed storing asset metadata in YAML inside GitLab. The format was readable enough for designers and maintainers to review, while remaining easy for the application to parse and version alongside each asset.

blocks.text: I built and tested the proof of concept in Vue

I moved from wireframes into a working Vue interface connected to the GitLab repository through an API. Using live asset records made the usability testing more credible, exposed technical assumptions that static screens would have hidden and allowed the proof of concept to be used internally for 30 days.

blocks.text: During the first 30 days of internal use, search and download time improved by 94%. Traffic increased by 78% compared with the previous repository and users downloaded 43 assets from an initial library of 100 icons.

blocks.text: Two product teams also reported that design debt fell from 57% to 21%. That observation came from those teams rather than a portfolio-wide measurement, but it suggested that making approved assets easier to find could reduce the temptation to recreate them.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.text: Search quality was not a layer added to the interface. It depended on the language, metadata and ownership model underneath it.
